title: Sustainability Is Not an Add-On. It’s a Foundation.
descriptions:
Buildings always leave an impact. The real question is, what kind of impact are we choosing to leave behind?


For Gujarat’s real estate developer, Shivalik Group, sustainability is not treated as an extra feature added at the end of a project. It is part of the way projects are planned, designed, built, and delivered.


Since 2018, Shivalik Group has been growing with a clear sense of responsibility. Across different projects, the focus has remained consistent: save water, manage rainwater, treat waste responsibly, generate clean energy, reduce common area power dependency, and divert construction waste from landfills.


At Shivalik Avenue, 59.7 lakh litres of water are saved annually. At Shivalik Parkview 2, 95% of peak site runoff is captured. At Shivalik Sharda Harmony, a 225 KLD STP and 400 kg/day OWC help manage wastewater and organic waste within the system.


Shivalik Greenview generates 1.94 lakh kWh of energy every year through a 125 KWP solar system. Shivalik Edge supports 100% of its common area lighting load through solar. Shivalik Platinum saves 14,560 litres of water daily. Shivalik Enclave has diverted 29,350 kg of construction waste from landfills.

These are not just technical numbers. They reflect a larger mindset.


Real estate today cannot only be judged by elevation, location, amenities, or price. The next layer of value is responsibility. How much water does a building save? How efficiently does it use energy? How does it manage waste? How much pressure does it reduce from the city’s larger infrastructure?


Every project may be different, but the responsibility remains the same.

Water saved.

Rain captured.

Waste managed.

Energy generated.

Power used responsibly.

Landfill load reduced.

That is how Shivalik Group is growing responsibly.


Because responsible real estate is not only about what we build today. It is also about the impact we leave for tomorrow.
author: Chitrak Shah

title: Ahmedabad Is Moving to Zero-Tolerance Roads
descriptions:
Ahmedabad is not just fixing traffic.

It is restructuring how the city moves.


A new policy is being prepared to unclog city roads,

with a clear shift towards stricter enforcement, better planning, and technology-led traffic management.


At first glance, this looks like a mobility upgrade.

But in real estate, this is something much bigger.


WHAT IS CHANGING

• Redesign of key junctions

• Real-time traffic control systems

• Zero tolerance on encroachments

• Structured parking infrastructure

• Strong push for public transport and walkability


Along with this, select corridors will be developed as “zero-tolerance roads”.

Clean. Organised. Enforced.


Real estate does not grow only on location.

It grows on access, movement, and usability of that location.

And this policy directly impacts all three.


WHAT HAPPENS TO MICRO-MARKETS

Corridors that get this level of intervention will see:

• Faster connectivity

• Better street experience

• Improved perception of the area

• Higher demand from both end-users and investors


Because when roads become efficient,

the radius of convenience expands.


And when convenience expands,

pricing follows.


This also changes how development is evaluated.

• Frontage quality becomes more important

• Accessibility becomes a premium factor

• Organised infrastructure attracts organised capital


Unplanned growth starts getting filtered out.


The biggest opportunity is not after everything is built.

It is before the transformation fully reflects in pricing.

Because once a corridor becomes structured and enforceable,

it rarely goes back.


This is not a traffic policy.

This is a corridor-level urban upgrade.


And in real estate,

corridor upgrades quietly create the next pricing cycles.
author: Chitrak Shah

title: The 20–50% Cost Surge Changing Everything
descriptions:
Cement, steel, tiles, aluminium - up 20–50%.

Projects were planned on stable costs, fixed timelines, and predictable margins.


Today, that assumption is breaking.

Global disruptions are pushing construction costs up ~20%.

And availability is becoming a challenge, not just pricing.


Which is now reflecting across the system:

• Project timelines extending (up to 6 months)

• Property prices set to rise

• Cashflow and execution pressure increasing

• Smaller developers will feel the impact first


WHY THIS IS HAPPENING

• Global supply chain disruptions driven by geopolitical conflicts

• Increase in energy and logistics costs

• Export–import imbalance in key raw materials

• Demand recovering faster than supply in real estate


So what is the industry doing?

There is no single fix.


Developers are focusing on what they can control:

• Optimising design and reducing wastage

• Strengthening procurement and sourcing strategies

• Managing launches and execution timelines more tightly

• Absorbing part of the cost, while passing the rest


At a policy level, there is a push for:

• Faster approvals

• GST rationalisation

• Better access to capital

• Stronger affordability support


Because the real issue is not just cost.

It is how the system operates under pressure.


INDUSTRY BENEFIT (LONG-TERM)

• Filters out unorganised and undercapitalised developers

• Pushes standardisation, better planning, and cost discipline

• Encourages innovation in construction technology and sourcing

• Strengthens serious players with strong execution and governance


Real estate doesn’t move only on demand.

It moves on cost, execution, and supply chain stability.

Right now, all 3 are under pressure.


FOR STAKEHOLDERS

Buyers: Expect price corrections. Waiting may not make it cheaper.

Developers: Procurement strategy and efficiency will define survival.

Investors: Early entry into under-construction assets becomes critical.


This is not a short-term spike.

This is a cost-driven shift in real estate.

title: The Ahmedabad Metro is no longer something you read about in a project timeline.
descriptions:
It is running.

Phase II is fully commissioned now. The final stretch connecting through to Mahatma Mandir went live at the start of this year, completing a network that links Ahmedabad, Gandhinagar, and GIFT City in a single continuous system.


For most people reading this, that reads like an infrastructure update. I think it is a buying signal.


Here is what actually changes when a metro stops being "upcoming" and starts being operational. Buyers who were sitting out, waiting for confirmation before committing to a corridor, no longer have a reason to wait. The confirmation just arrived. Which means the next phase of demand is not speculative. It is backed by a physical, running transit system that anyone can test themselves.


Vaishnodevi Circle sits within reach of this network. The corridor already had the road infrastructure, the ring road access, the proximity to GIFT City employment. What it did not have was a metro story people fully believed in.

That story is now done.


The reason this matters more than people are letting on is because transit connectivity does not just serve the people who use public transport. It changes how the entire corridor is valued. Rental yields improve because working professionals prioritise metro-linked areas. Resale liquidity improves because the buyer pool deepens. Institutional interest follows because the location thesis is no longer dependent on optimism.


I have watched corridors in other Indian cities go through this exact sequence. Speculation ahead of the metro. A quiet period as people wait. Then a visible re-rating once the trains are actually running and people realise the commute times are real.

North Ahmedabad is in that third phase now.


What is interesting is that Vaishnodevi Circle specifically sits at the junction of two major arterials, SP Ring Road and SG Highway. The metro adds a third layer of connectivity on top of road infrastructure that was already strong. That combination is not common in any city, let alone at the price points this corridor currently trades at.


The buyers who acted twelve months ago knew something the market is only now confirming.

The buyers acting today still know something the market will only fully confirm twelve months from now.

That window does not stay open indefinitely.

When infrastructure is promised, prices move partly. When infrastructure is delivered, prices move fully. The gap between those two moments is where every good real estate decision gets made.

Ahmedabad just delivered. North Ahmedabad just got re-rated.

The question worth asking is not whether this area will appreciate. The question is whether you want to be on the right side of the next confirmation.

This shift changes everything:

→ Better quality control

→ Reduced cost leakages

→ Higher transparency for buyers and investors


Real estate is no longer just about building structures.

title: A New Era of Verified Land Ownership
descriptions:
Stronger Systems. Cleaner Transactions.

A significant step forward for Gujarat’s real estate ecosystem.


The state has now made 25-year historical land records mandatory for farm land transactions. At first glance, it may seem like tighter regulation but in reality, this is a move toward trust, transparency, and long-term stability.

Here’s what it changes:


• Clear ownership history → reduces disputes and title risks

• Verified farmer status → ensures compliance with regulations

• Structured approvals → incomplete or unclear applications won’t pass through

• Defined recourse window (30 days) → adds fairness and accountability

For years, agricultural land transactions have faced one core issue: lack of structured verification.


This move directly addresses that gap.

What this means for the industry:

→ Serious investors gain confidence

→ Speculative or unclear deals get filtered out

→ Land becomes a more credible, institutional asset class

→ Long-term planning becomes easier for developers and funds


This is not restriction.

This is standardization of a fragmented layer of real estate.

And every time real estate becomes more structured,

capital flows improve, risks reduce, and the ecosystem matures.


A step closer to building

A system-driven real estate market - not transaction-driven.

title: The Art of Quiet Luxury
descriptions:
You worked hard. Built something. Made the right moves. Reached where you wanted to.


And now, after years of chasing, you have learned something.


The loudest rooms are not the ones you want to be in.

The busiest weekends are not the ones you remember.

The things that used to excite you? They feel different now.


You find yourself looking for quiet.

Not silence, just peace.

A place where you do not have to perform.

Where the only thing expected of you is to breathe.


If this sounds familiar, you already understand what true luxury is.


It is the space where the morning light falls exactly where you want to sit with your coffee.

It is the space where you feel most yourself.


True luxury is not about being seen. It is about how deeply you can feel at ease.


Think about the people you know who have truly settled into their lives.

After a long week, where do they go? Not to crowded places. Not to events where they have to be "on."

They go to the mountains. To a quiet retreat. To a spot by the water where no one is calling their name.


They have earned the right to choose. And what they choose, again and again, is stillness.


Now here is the question for you.


When you come home after a long day, not a vacation, just a Tuesday

does your home give you that same feeling? Does it let you let go? Or does it demand something from you?


Here is what I have learned from watching people who have built their lives well.


The ones who truly understand luxury do not chase it. They curate it.


So when you are settling down,

truly settling, not just buying a house, ask yourself different questions.


  • "How will I feel when I walk through the door?"
  • "Will this space let me think?"
  • "Will this be the place I never want to leave?"


Because the people who have done it all, seen it all, built it all

they are not looking for more. They are looking for a place to put it all down.


A place where footsteps are softer.

Conversations are slower.

Even a glass is placed gently, so the moment is not disturbed.

title: I've Watched Both Types Up Close. Here's the Real Difference.
descriptions:
CS on the difference between being rich and being wealthy

and why most people are chasing the wrong thing.


He walked into a room.

Asked the people there: "What's the difference between rich and wealthy?"


He got answers. Different ones. Interesting ones.

But none of them matched what he actually believes.


So here's what CS really thinks, and honestly, once you hear it, you can't unhear it.


Rich people are busy. Wealthy people are free.

That's the short version.

But let's actually sit with it.


A rich person has figured out how to make money. Real money. Enough to be proud of.


But here's the catch: they're doing everything themselves.

The planning. The execution. The follow-up. Every single thing.

They're talented. They're capable. They're... exhausted.


Because when you do everything yourself, the business doesn't run without you.

You're not the CEO. You're the engine.


Wealthy is a completely different game.

The wealthy person starts with a vision.

Not a task list. Not a project plan. A vision.


Something big. Something that can't be done alone.

And they know that from the beginning.


So they hire people who believe in that vision.

People who are good at those things.

People who can take that vision and run with it.


And then, this is the part most people miss

they step back.


Not because they're lazy. Because that's the whole point.

They set themselves free. So they can think. So they can build the next vision.


Why this works

When you're doing everything, your growth has a ceiling.

That ceiling is you. Your hours. Your energy. Your bandwidth.


But when you build a team around a vision? The ceiling disappears.

Because now 10 people are running. Then 20. Then 50.


CS talks about this specifically: the wealthy person doesn't just grow themselves.

They build 50 people like themselves.

Think about that.


One person becomes a multiplier.

They carry the thinking, the vision, the culture

and they plant it in others.

That's not just wealth. That's legacy.


What most people do wrong

They confuse being busy with being productive.


They wear busyness like a badge. "I'm handling everything."

That feels like control. It feels like responsibility.


But what it actually is: it is a trap.


The second mistake? They think hiring is a cost.

It's not. Hiring the right people is the actual investment.


The third mistake and this one's quiet, is that they never define the vision.

They just work. Day after day. Project after project. Without ever asking: where is all of this going?


A rich person is always answering the question of today.

A wealthy person is always answering the question of ten years from now.


The perspective shift


Here's what CS's thinking really boils down to.


Rich is about what you can do.

Wealthy is about what you can build.


Rich is solo. Wealthy is a movement.


The rich person leaves when they stop working.

The wealthy person has already left, and the work kept growing.


The goal isn't to be the hardest worker in the room.

The goal is to build a room full of people who carry your vision further than you ever could alone.

title: Which Area to Invest? CS's Simple Framework
descriptions:
People often ask CS: where should I invest?


His answer is simple. And it goes against what most people think.


He says: look for areas that are 20-30% developed.


Not too early. Not too late.


At 20-30%, the area does not look fully ready.

The roads may still be being built. The shops are not all open.

It does not feel like a premium address yet.


But that is exactly the point.


Why 20-30%?


Because that is when the growth has started but not peaked.

The infrastructure is coming. The prices have begun to move.

But the premium has not been fully priced in.


If you buy at this stage, you enter before the crowd.

You get the growth that comes as the area develops from 30% to 80-90%.


What about the other end?


If you do not want to take risk, if you want safety and certainty

you can invest in areas that are 80-90% developed.


These areas are established. The roads are built.

The markets are thriving. You know what you are getting.


But the return will not be the same.

Most of the growth has already happened.

You are paying for certainty, not upside.


The trade-off is simple:


20-30% developed = higher risk, higher return.


80-90% developed = lower risk, lower return.


What most people do wrong?


They buy at 0-10% development. Too early. Too much uncertainty.

They wait years for the area to catch up.

Or they buy at 80-90% development and wonder why their investment did not grow as fast as they expected.


CS says: the sweet spot is in the middle. 20-30% developed.


How do you find it?


Look for areas where the basic rates have started moving from ₹2,500–3,000 per sq ft to ₹3,500–4,500 per sq ft.

Development is visible but not complete. Infrastructure is coming. People are starting to notice.


The area may not look appealing at first. That is the sign.


Because the areas that look fully ready today?

You are paying for what someone else saw ten years ago.


The areas that are 20-30% developed today?

You are paying for what you will see ten years from now.


Key Insights:


  • CS's framework: invest in areas that are 20-30% developed, not too early, not too late.
  • At this stage, growth has started but the premium is not fully priced in.
  • 80-90% developed areas are safer, but returns are lower.
  • 0-10% developed areas carry too much uncertainty and waiting time.

title: Building the Strategy from the Ground Up
descriptions:
We are launching our fourth project at GIFT City.

RERA registered. Ready to go.

But this one is different.


The positioning is different. The audience is entirely different.

So before anything goes to market: I sat my team down.


"Build me the entire strategy. How we sell. Who we sell to. Everything mapped. From scratch.


They came back prepared.

Started the pitch the way they always do.

Amenities. Features. Specifications. The usual.

I stopped them.


"I can change amenities. I can upgrade features. I can integrate whatever facility you're describing. Give me something else. Why should I buy this?"


Silence.


Not because they didn't know the project.

Because they had never been asked that question before.


I was asking them to sell what isn't.

That silence told me everything.

Because here's the real problem

If you don't know why someone should buy this, you will go to the wrong people.


And the wrong audience is not just a missed sale.

It's a problem that follows you through the entire lifecycle of the project.

Wrong buyer asks the wrong questions.

Negotiates on the wrong things.

Creates the wrong energy in the building.

And tells the wrong people about it.


Ultra-luxury is not a product category.

It's a mindset category.

The person buying at this level is not looking for a deal.

They want something rare.


The lesson is simple.

Selling ultra-luxury is not about selling.

It's about selecting.

The right buyer, the right positioning, the right story.

When those three align, the conversation is easy.

When they don't:

no amenity, no feature, no offer will fix it.


Get the audience wrong and everything else you do is noise.

Go back to the ground.

Understand who you're actually talking to.


Then build the pitch around them: not around the project.

Because the project is ready. The question is: who is it ready for?

title: Why "Exclusive" Works Better Than "Expensive"
descriptions:
In real estate, how you position a home matters more than anything.


Most agents make the same mistake:

They start talking about features. Size. Price. Amenities.


But for ultra-luxury, none of that comes first.


The right way sounds like this:


  • "We are not offering this apartment to just anyone.
  • "Homes like this are not built for general sale."
  • "Owning a home of this quality is a privilege: one we offer only to someone who truly understands what makes it special."


Why does this work?


Because homes of this level are not just sold. They create an opportunity.

They are meant for a select few: people who value the lifestyle, the network, the way the home makes them feel.


Features? Secondary.

Price? Secondary.


What matters first? Pride.

The pride of owning something rare.

Something not available anywhere else.

Something only you can have.


Here is what I have learned:


Sell to the wrong person and you will get the wrong result.

Every time.


Before you talk price or floor plan,

know exactly who you are talking to.


If you sell a luxury home like a normal home,

you will lose the sale before it even starts.


Position it as a privilege.

Sell the exclusivity.

Then show them the home.


Insight by Chitrak Shah | Shivalik Group


#UltraLuxury #RealEstateSales #Positioning #Exclusivity #ShivalikGroup
author: Chitrak Shah

title: What Buyers Won't Tell You (But Will Decide)
descriptions:
For decades, the Indian buyer asked one question: can I afford this?


In 2026, they are asking something different: is this worth it?


That is not a small shift. It is a complete change in how real estate must be designed, delivered, and experienced.


What changed?


Earlier, affordability was everything.

If the price fit the budget, the home was considered.

Features, quality, long-term value: those were secondary.

The buyer was buying a roof.


Now, the buyer is buying a life.

A home that will hold its value.

A community that will age well.

A developer they can trust for decades, not just until possession.


The market doesn't reward the best product.

It rewards the most trusted standard.


Think about it. Two homes. Similar size. Similar location. Similar price.

One is built by a developer who delivers on time, communicates honestly, and thinks beyond the handover.

The other is built by someone who promises the moon and delivers a rock.


Which one sells? Which one holds value?

Which one will the buyer recommend to their children?


This is the shift.


Trust is no longer a nice-to-have.

It is the only thing that matters.


Buyers today have choices.

They have information.

They have seen too many projects delayed, too many promises broken, too many families left waiting.


They are not just buying square feet. They are buying peace of mind.


What this means for developers:


If you build only for today, you will be forgotten tomorrow.


If you build for trust,consistent quality, honest communication, long-term thinking,

you become the standard.

And the standard is what buyers return to. Again and again.


The question is no longer: can they afford it?


It is: can they trust it?


Insight by Chitrak Shah | Shivalik Group


#TrustMatters #RealEstateShift #BuiltToLast #StandardNotProduct #ShivalikGroup
author: Chitrak Shah

title: What Makes a City Worth Remembering?
descriptions:
Skylines are not accidents.


They are the sum of a thousand decisions nobody photographed.


Each decision, small.

But together, they become a city.


The cities that will matter globally in 2040 are not the ones that built the most.


They are the ones that built with intention: knowing exactly what they were creating.


The cities we admire today: the ones with character, with soul, with longevity,

were not built by accident.


They were built by developers who thought beyond their own timeline.

Who made decisions not for the next quarter, but for the next generation.


Ahmedabad is being built right now.


Every project, every road, every decision is adding to its skyline.

The question is: are we building with intention? Or are we just building?


Because 20 years from now, we will look at this city.

And we will see exactly what we decided today.


Isight by Chitrak Shah | Shivalik Group


#SkylinesAreNotAccidents #BuildWithIntention #CityBuilding #LongTermThinking #ShivalikGroup
author: Chitrak Shah

title: Most businesses fail because  fragmentation
descriptions:
Most businesses don’t fail because of competition.

They fail because the experience is fragmented.


Recently, this became very clear to us.


In a single day,

one family, the uncle bought two premium apartments.


They are an NRI family,

planning their move back to India.


Both homes were bought with furniture.


Why does this matter for entrepreneurs?


Because the decision wasn’t driven by pricing.

It was driven by convenience and clarity.


Everything was available in one ecosystem:

homes, interiors, furniture, timelines, paperwork.


One decision.

One flow.

Zero friction.


This is the same reason platforms like Swiggy or Zepto scale so fast.


Not because they sell food or groceries,

but because they remove effort from the customer’s life.


Entrepreneurs often try to scale by:

• increasing marketing

• pushing harder sales

• adding more features


But scale actually comes from integration.


When you can offer a 360° solution,

customers don’t compare,

they commit.


That’s the real power of ecosystem thinking.


If you’re building a business today,

ask yourself:

Are you selling a product,

or are you designing a seamless experience?


Because smooth experiences don’t just convert better.


They scale faster.
author: Chitrak Shah

title: “Investor trust” is a #myth.
descriptions:
“Investor trust” is a #myth.


Recently, on a podcast, a young boy asked me:

“How do you build investor trust?”


My answer was simple & practical,


In investing, there is no trust.

There is only transparency.


Real #investing is not about hype, storytelling, or optimism.

It’s about clarity,

#governance, and clean numbers.


Put everything on the table.


• Show the real profit

• Show the real margin

• Show what is shareable

• Show the risks upfront


This is how serious,

#investors, #institutionalcapital,

And long-term partners think.


If the outcome matches what you committed,

trust follows automatically.


Whether you’re selling

real estate, gold, or even stone,


Say exactly what you are doing.

Do exactly what you said.


That’s not trust-building.

That’s credibility.


And credibility compounds,

in business, #leadership, investing, and reputation.


One non-negotiable rule:

Outcome must match commitment.
author: Chitrak Shah

title: Decoding Real Estate Growth Signals
descriptions:
Real estate growth is not always visible in reports.

It is visible on the ground.


Smart investors don’t wait for price appreciation.

They track early signals.


One of the most underrated indicators:

Vehicle registration growth.


When an area starts growing, the first visible change is movement.

More people. More income. More consumption.


And it reflects directly in:

  • Increase in new car registrations
  • Higher presence of premium vehicles
  • Parking pressure in residential and commercial zones

Because car buying is not random.


It is linked to income confidence and lifestyle upgrade.

But this is just one layer.


Serious investors map growth using multiple on-ground signals:

1. Vehicle density trend (year-on-year)

Rising registrations = rising economic activity


2. Rental movement

If rents are increasing steadily, demand is real, not speculative


3. Retail expansion

New cafes, brands, showrooms entering = spending power rising


4. Traffic pattern change

More peak-hour congestion = higher daily movement = higher relevance


5. Construction intensity

Number of active sites = developer confidence in the micro-market


Growth does not start with price.

It starts with behavior.

Prices follow what people start doing consistently.


If you want to invest early,

stop tracking just property rates.

Start tracking how people are moving, earning, and spending in that area.
author: Chitrak Shah

title: Where Real Estate Stands Today
descriptions:
Real estate today is no longer in an early growth phase.

It is entering a more structured, performance-driven cycle.

The market has evolved across four clear shifts.


1. From speculation to structured investing

Earlier cycles were driven by land bets and price gaps.

Today, capital is becoming more disciplined.


Investors are evaluating:

  • Cash flows
  • Exit visibility
  • Developer credibility

The mindset is shifting from “buy and wait” to “buy with a strategy.”


2. From product selling to ecosystem building

Projects are no longer competing on units.

They are competing on complete environments.

  • Integrated communities
  • Work-live ecosystems
  • Lifestyle + functionality

Standalone developments are slowly losing relevance.


3. From unorganized to branded developers

Trust has become a core currency.

Buyers and investors are moving toward:

  • Proven developers
  • Consistent delivery track record
  • Governance and transparency

Brand is now directly linked to valuation.


4. From local demand to capital-driven markets

The market is no longer purely end-user driven.

  • HNI / UHNI participation is increasing
  • Institutional capital is entering
  • NRI investments are rising

Real estate is becoming an asset class, not just a purchase decision.


This is not a slowdown.

This is a filtering phase.

Stronger projects, better developers, and smarter investors will define the next cycle.


Real estate is no longer about entering the market.

It is about understanding which phase of the market you are entering.
author: Chitrak Shah

title: What Actually Compounds Property Value
descriptions:
Real estate appreciation is often misattributed to location and timing.

In reality, long-term value is engineered through a combination of structural, economic, and behavioral factors that most buyers overlook.

The strongest drivers are rarely visible at first glance.


1. Micro-positioning within a macro location

Value is created not just by the area, but by precise placement within it.

Access, frontage, entry-exit flow, and adjacency to future movement corridors determine long-term demand intensity.


2. Land economics and development discipline

Projects built on strong land fundamentals outperform consistently.

Lower density, better planning ratios, and long-term land control create assets that age well and retain premium positioning.


3. Alignment with future infrastructure

Appreciation is a forward-looking function.

Capital flows where infrastructure is planned, not where it is already saturated.

Early alignment with roads, transit, and commercial corridors creates asymmetric upside.


4. Developer philosophy and execution consistency

Markets assign premium to predictability.

Developers who build ecosystems, not isolated projects, create compounding value across phases and locations.

Trust translates into liquidity and price resilience.


5. Exit liquidity architecture

An asset’s value is only as strong as its ability to transact.

Ticket size, buyer profile alignment, and market depth determine whether appreciation can be realized or remains theoretical.


6. Product relevance across time cycles

Assets that adapt to changing user behavior sustain value.

Efficient layouts, usable amenities, and functional design outperform trend-driven offerings over long horizons.


7. Social and community layer

Often underestimated, but critical.

Communities with strong resident profiles and governance standards create self-reinforcing demand and protect long-term asset value.


Appreciation is not a single event.

It is a designed outcome of multiple aligned variables over time.


In institutional real estate thinking,

value is not found.

It is built, positioned, and exited strategically.
author: Chitrak Shah

title: Sustainability Is Built, Not Added
descriptions:
Sustainability in housing is often reduced to features.

Solar panels, certifications, surface-level green elements.

But in reality, sustainability is a design decision taken on day zero.


It is embedded in how a home is planned, positioned, and performs over decades.

A truly sustainable home operates as an efficient system:

  • Climate-responsive design : orientation, shading, and airflow reduce dependency on artificial cooling
  • Resource efficiency : optimized water usage, energy consumption, and waste management
  • Spatial intelligence : layouts that minimize dead space and maximize usability
  • Material longevity : choices that reduce lifecycle costs, not just upfront aesthetics


This is not about lowering impact alone.

It is about enhancing performance, for both the resident and the asset.


Because over time:

  • Lower operational costs improve affordability
  • Better living conditions improve health and productivity
  • Smarter planning improves long-term relevance and resale value

And this is where the market is quietly shifting.


The question is no longer:

“How big is the home?”


The question is:

“How efficiently does this home perform over the next 20 years?”

That is the real benchmark of sustainability.


Because in real estate,

what sustains over time… creates value over time.
author: Chitrak Shah

title: First Home: Think Like an Investor
descriptions:
Your first home is not just a milestone.

It is likely your largest financial decision (₹50L–₹2Cr+).

Most buyers optimise for emotion.

Experts optimise for numbers, risk, and liquidity.


1. Micro-Market Trajectory

Real estate returns are location-driven.

  • Emerging corridors can deliver 8–12% CAGR
  • Mature areas often settle at 3–6% CAGR

Check infra planned in the next 3–5 years.

Growth follows infrastructure, not marketing.


2. Developer Execution Quality

Execution directly impacts your returns.

  • Average project delays in India: 12–24 months
  • Delay impact: EMI + rent = ₹3–8L extra burden

Always check past delivery, not just brand recall.


3. Legal & Structural Risk

One mistake here can freeze your capital.

  • Legal disputes can delay possession by 3–5 years
  • RERA-registered projects reduce risk significantly

Never skip due diligence.


4. Financial Structuring

Your EMI is not your real cost.

  • A ₹75L home can cost ₹1.2–1.4Cr over loan tenure
  • Safe EMI rule: ≤ 30–35% of your monthly income
  • Keep 6 months emergency buffer

Over-leverage is the biggest mistake.


5. Product-Market Fit

Liquidity depends on demand.

  • 2–3 BHK units drive 70–80% of resale demand in most markets
  • Right ticket size = faster resale

If the market doesn’t need it, exit becomes slow.


6. Exit Liquidity

Real estate is not always liquid.

  • Average resale cycle: 3–9 months
  • In weak markets, can extend beyond 12 months

Strong broker + investor network reduces exit time significantly.


7. Ecosystem Impact

Location convenience directly affects value.

  • Properties near strong infra see 10–25% price premium
  • Rental demand increases by 15–30% in well-connected zones

You don’t live inside your house.

You live in its ecosystem.


First-time buyers often mix lifestyle and investment without clarity.

But the reality is simple:

  • Wrong decision can lock your capital for 5–10 years
  • Right decision compounds quietly over time 


Because in real estate,

you don’t just buy a home.

You enter a long-term financial position.
author: Chitrak Shah

title: Workspaces That Change Output
descriptions:
Workspaces are not just places to sit.

They directly influence how people think, feel, and perform.


Low-quality, cluttered environments reduce focus.

Average buildings create average output.

But high-rise, well-designed, iconic buildings change behavior.


They create:

  • Mental elevation : People think bigger in better spaces
  • Higher energy : Natural light, openness, views improve focus
  • Professional identity : Teams feel part of something larger
  • Client perception : First impression becomes stronger than any pitch

This is where iconic developments make the difference.


Take Shivalik Wave as an example.

It is not just about height.

It is about how the building is designed to improve the way businesses operate.

  • Premium work environment
  • Strategic location advantage
  • Elevated design and visibility
  • A space that reflects ambition

Because serious businesses don’t just choose offices.

They choose environments that push them to perform better.


The real shift is this:

Companies are no longer asking, “What is the cost per sq.ft.?”

They are asking, “What is the value this space creates?”

And that is where iconic buildings win.


Because in business,

your environment is not a background.

It is a growth driver.
author: Chitrak Shah

title: Entry Matters. Exit Builds Wealth.
descriptions:
Real estate is not about buying property.

It is about entering right and exiting smart.


Most people only focus on location.

Serious investors focus on the full cycle.


Entry decides your potential.

Right entry means lower risk, better upside, stronger ROI.

Wrong entry means stuck capital, slow growth, limited returns.


Exit decides your wealth.

Profit is not made on paper.

It is made when you successfully exit at the right time.

And this is where most people struggle.

Because exit is not just timing.


Exit is about access.

  • Access to the right buyer
  • Access to the right network
  • Access to liquidity when you need it

Without a strong network, even a good asset can stay unsold.

That’s why expert guidance becomes critical.

Experts don’t just help you buy.

They help you position, hold, and exit strategically.

They understand cycles.

They understand demand shifts.

They know when to enter and more importantly, when to step out.


Real wealth in real estate is created by three things:

Right Entry

Right Exit

Right Network

If one is missing, returns get compromised.

Because in real estate,

you don’t just invest in property.

You invest in timing, strategy, and people.
author: Chitrak Shah

title: Why Most People Enter Real Estate the Wrong Way?
descriptions:
Everyone wants to get into real estate. It's where serious money gets made.


But most people get it wrong from the start.


They come in for the wrong reason.

They see a deal close, they see the commission, they see the price appreciation and they think, "I want that."

If it's only money you're after, real estate is probably not for you. There are faster ways to make money. Stock trading. Land flipping. Businesses that turn over capital quickly.


Real estate is a long game.

It's about what you create.


The family that moves into your home and lives better.

The neighbourhood that becomes a community because someone thought about it carefully.

If that does not excite you: the creation, the impact, the responsibility, the money will feel hollow when it comes.


So how do you build a real career here?

First, learn. Spend three to four years understanding how projects are built, how customers think.

Because your early mistakes are not just yours. Someone's home their biggest purchase is on the line.


Then, pick a lane. Real estate is design, construction, finance, tech, management.

Find what you're good at. Go deep for at least three years.


And stay focused. The biggest trap is distraction. Social media shows you fifteen ways to make money every day.

The people who build real careers are the ones who picked a direction and stayed long enough to actually get good.


We've seen this for 25 years.

The people who stayed, learned, and committed, they built something real.

That's why we built an institute. Not just to train people for jobs, but to build professionals with the right mindset from day one.


Insights:

  • Real estate is a long game. Fast money chasers should look elsewhere.
  • Your early mistakes affect real families. Learn before you leap.
  • Pick one lane and stay in it. Depth beats breadth.
  • Distraction is the biggest trap. Focus builds careers.


Great people are not made overnight.

They are built through the right experiences, mentors, and mindset.

Real estate in India is growing fast. But the quality of people entering it will determine if that growth lasts.


Build yourself the same way you would build a home. With the right foundation.


Insight by CS | Crafting Bharat - Gujarat Edition (YT)


#Entrepreneurship #CareerAdvice #RealEstate #MindsetMatters #ShivalikGroup
author: Chitrak Shah

title: Viksit Bharat is Built on Infrastructure
descriptions:
You cannot build a city without building the foundation first.


Roads are built.

Then buildings come up.

Then communities form.

Only then do we call it a developed area.


This is the sequence every major city has followed: from New York to Dubai to Mumbai.

Real estate does not create development. It follows infrastructure. And then it accelerates everything around it.


Speaking on Crafting Bharat Gujarat Edition, Chitrak Shah Sir put it simply: "Real estate is the first thing that enters after infrastructure.

And without it, a Viksit Bharat is simply not possible."


This matters enormously right now. With the 2030 Commonwealth Games and a potential 2036 Olympics on the horizon for Ahmedabad,infrastructure timelines

that were planned for a decade are being compressed into four years.

Roads, hotels, transit everything is being fast-tracked.


What was a possibility is now a certainty.

And real estate sits directly in the path of that acceleration.


Key Insights:


  • Infrastructure de-risks real estate investment. When the government commits to large-scale events, surrounding development becomes inevitable, not speculative.
  • Investors who wait for full clarity often enter after the best appreciation has already happened.
  • Gujarat is structurally positioned, not just politically favoured. GIFT City, Dholera, and Ahmedabad together form an infrastructure corridor that few Indian cities can match today.


Strategic Insight:


The most durable real estate markets are not built on hype. They are built on sequencing.

When infrastructure investment precedes and exceeds real estate supply, prices follow with conviction.

Ahmedabad is currently in that window.
author: Chitrak Shah

title: Most Developers Leave After Possession. We Stay.
descriptions:
For decades, Indian real estate followed a simple model:

build,

sell,

move on.


The developer’s role ended at possession.


What followed was left to the buyer.

Maintenance issues.

Repairs.

Interiors.

Society management.

Different people. Different systems. No continuity.


Homeownership, which should have been a source of stability, often became a source of friction.

This is the gap.

A home is not a transaction.

It is a 40–50 year relationship between a family and the space they live in.


If the developer exits at handover,

the buyer is left managing a lifecycle they were never designed to handle alone.

The response to this is not incremental.

It is structural.


Not more services.

An ecosystem.

Maintenance.

Interiors.

Community management.

Investment pathways.

Education.

All integrated.

All accessible through one relationship.

Enabled through a single digital layer: the R app.


Because the goal is not to improve the buying moment.

It is to simplify the living experience.


This is where the model shifts.


From transaction

to continuity.

From delivery

to responsibility.

From selling homes

to staying relevant in how people live inside them.

And once that shift happens, everything compounds.


Trust deepens.

Referrals become natural.

Reinvestment becomes easier.


The product is no longer just the home.

It is the experience that follows it.


Key Insights:


  • Post-possession is no longer an afterthought. It is part of the product itself.
  • Buyers are beginning to evaluate developers based on long-term experience, not just delivery quality.
  • Ecosystem-led models create compounding trust, not one-time transactions.


Strategic Insight:


The next decade in real estate will not be defined by who builds the most.

It will be defined by who stays the longest.

Because in a 40-year relationship,

possession is not the end.

It is the starting point.
author: Chitrak Shah

title: India’s Home Buying Age Has Shifted
descriptions:
In the 1990s, people bought homes at 45 - 55.

Today, most Indians are buying between 28 - 35.

That’s not a small change.

That’s a 15–20 year shift in one generation.


What the data shows

  • ~60–65% home buyers are under 35
  • Average first-time buying age: 28–35
  • Home loan demand: 50%+ from 25–34 age group

India has moved from

“buy after stability” → “buy while building stability.”


Why this shift happened

1. Credit became easier

Earlier you needed savings.

Now you need eligibility.


2. Dual income households

Two salaries = higher affordability.


3. Rent vs EMI mindset

Owning feels like building an asset.

Rent feels like an expense.


4. Lifestyle aspiration

Homes are no longer basic.

They are gated, designed, experience-driven.


5. Real estate = investment

Not just “ghar”

→ asset

→ appreciation

→ rental income


How people are buying today

  • 70–80% purchases are loan-driven
  • 20–30 year EMIs are normal
  • Joint buying (husband-wife) is common
  • Entry happening in under-construction & emerging areas


But here’s the real gap

People are buying earlier.

But not always smarter.

  • Wrong location
  • No purpose clarity
  • Over-stretched EMIs


Early buying without clarity becomes pressure.

Late buying without action becomes regret.


So what’s the right age?

There is no number.

Buy when:

  • Your income is stable
  • EMI is under control
  • City decision is clear
  • Purpose is defined


India didn’t start buying homes earlier because people became richer.

It happened because credit became easier and aspirations became bigger.
author: Chitrak Shah

title: ₹5,050 Cr Infra Trigger
descriptions:
Motera - Chandkheda was already on the map,

Driven by proximity to Narendra Modi Stadium, metro access, and improving connectivity.


But it was still missing a strong lifestyle and ecosystem driver to push it into the next league.

Now that changes.


AMC is fast-tracking the ₹5,050 crore Sardar Patel Sports Enclave by reallocating land and accelerating execution.


This is not just a development.

It’s a city-scale infrastructure anchor.

And when that happens, micro-markets don’t stay the same.


They shift.

You can expect:

• Demand to rise due to increased activity and footfall

• Rental potential to strengthen (events + workforce + visitors)

• Projects nearby to reposition towards premium

• Long-term appreciation as the ecosystem builds out


This is how real estate moves,

Not suddenly, but structurally.

Early signals are already visible.


The opportunity is not when everything is built.

The opportunity is when everything is being planned.

Track this micro-market closely.
author: Chitrak Shah

title: Why Community Sells Homes
descriptions:
In India, homes are not bought individually.

They are approved socially.


A buyer may shortlist based on price and location.

But the final decision depends on one question:

“Will we belong here?”


This is where community enters.


Language.

Food habits.

Festivals.

People around you.

These are not soft factors.


They are decision drivers.


Research shows home buying in India is deeply influenced by family and social networks.

Relatives, references and known communities play a direct role in closing decisions.


That’s why you see patterns:

Entire buildings filled through one network.

Societies dominated by one community.

Clusters where demand sustains itself for years.

Because trust travels through people.


One family buys.

3 more follow.


This is not marketing.

This is behaviour.


Community also defines daily life.

Where your children grow.

Who your neighbours are.

What your everyday environment feels like.


For most Indian families, this matters more than amenities.

Even from an investment lens:


Strong community presence creates stable demand.

Stable demand creates better liquidity.

Liquidity supports price appreciation.


Which means community is not just emotional.

It is economic.

The mistake many make is thinking real estate is about product.


It is not.

It is about people.

Because in India:


You don’t just buy a home.

You choose who you live with.


#RealEstate #IndianRealEstate #HomeBuying #ConsumerBehaviour #Community #Investment #Ahmedabad #HousingMarket #RealEstateInsights
author: Chitrak Shah

title: GIFT City Living Push
descriptions:
GIFT City is accelerating toward a complete live-work ecosystem.

20+ international hotels and restaurants expected within the next 12 months

Government approval for “Working and Living” model already in motion


Current ecosystem snapshot:

  • 30,000+ professionals working inside GIFT City
  • Majority still commuting daily from Ahmedabad and Gandhinagar
  • Only ~100 families currently residing within the city


What is changing:

  • Residential focus is increasing to reduce daily commute load
  • Policy support is shifting toward on-site living infrastructure
  • New approvals include hotels, retail, social spaces and public amenities


Upcoming developments:

  • Shopping malls and high street retail zones planned
  • Riverfront and garden spaces under development
  • Entertainment and social infrastructure being added


Market signal:

  • Daytime population is already strong
  • Nighttime economy is still underdeveloped
  • This gap creates opportunity


Investor implications:

  • Residential demand is in early stage with low current supply
  • Rental yield potential increases as workforce shifts to on-site living
  • Retail and hospitality assets benefit from first mover advantage


Price insight:

  • Commercial land transactions already touching high benchmark levels
  • Early entrants captured lower price bands
  • Next phase likely to see upward price movement
  • 30,000+ workforce with limited residential base is a clear imbalance


This imbalance drives the next growth cycle

GIFT City is transitioning from workplace cluster to full urban ecosystem
author: Chitrak Shah

title: GIFT City Consumption Signal
descriptions:
GIFT City is entering a consumption-driven growth phase.

20+ international standard restaurants expected within 12 months

Clear shift from pure office hub to live-work ecosystem


What investors should read from this:

• F&B entry signals rising disposable income inside the ecosystem

• High-income workforce density is increasing

• Stay duration of professionals will expand beyond office hours

• Daily consumption per capita is expected to grow


Ecosystem drivers already in place:

  • Top institutions supplying talent
  • Foreign universities entering pipeline
  • Government pushing “Working and Living” model
  • Capital movement signal:
  • Consumption follows income
  • Income follows employment clusters
  • Employment clusters follow policy and infrastructure


All 3 are aligning inside GIFT City.


What this means for investments:

  • Retail spaces gain early traction due to immediate cash flow
  • Grade A commercial strengthens with global tenant demand
  • Serviced apartments and rental housing see faster absorption


Early phase indicators:

  • 20+ F&B brands entering before full residential scale
  • Institutional ecosystem already active
  • Policy support focused on long-term retention


This is not late-stage growth

This is early consumption activation

Entry timing defines upside in GIFT City.
author: Chitrak Shah

title: Do You Know The Story Behind These 8 Masterpieces?
descriptions:
Do You Know The Story Behind These 8 Masterpieces?


Do you know Burj Khalifa?

Today it stands as the tallest building in the world.

But what most people see is the height.


What they don’t see is the years of vision,

Engineering, design thinking, and relentless effort behind it.


Because masterpieces are never built overnight.

They begin with an idea.


Then comes the first sketch the moment imagination begins to take shape.

And slowly, through years of design, planning, and execution…


From the first sketch… to the moment imagination becomes a masterpiece that adds identity to your address.

That is the journey of every iconic structure.


In real estate, great buildings are not just projects.

They become part of a city’s skyline and part of people’s lives.


Across Ahmedabad, we have placed hoardings,

Of our Shivalik masterpieces. But behind every structure is a story,

A story of vision, patience, and the courage to build something timeless.

Now I’m curious,


How many of you know the story behind these structures?

And how many of you own a space inside one of these masterpieces?
author: Chitrak Shah

title: Most developers are growing in revenue.
descriptions:
Most developers are growing in revenue.

But not in ease. Not in compounding.


There's a reason for that - and it's not the team.


2026 is the year that transition begins.

But transitions don't begin in declarations.


They begin in one specific moment where you see something work -

and you can never unsee it.


---

Look at your last three projects.


They delivered. Numbers were good.

Team worked hard. You're proud.


Now ask yourself honestly:

Was Project 3 structurally easier than Project 1?


For most developers, the honest answer is no.


The reason is that your experience lives in people - not in architecture.


Scaling effort is not the same as scaling capability.

One exhausts you. The other builds without you.

---

The real shift isn't just inside your project. It's outside too.


India is at an inflection point that most developers haven't fully processed.

Institutional capital is entering Indian real estate at a scale and speed that demands governance.


The audience for what you build has fundamentally changed.

And that audience does not evaluate projects.

It evaluates systems.


It asks:

Does this developer have documented execution standards?

Verifiable governance?

Consistent quality across cities or just on their home ground?


Personality-led execution cannot answer those questions.

Operating architecture can.


---

Every project felt like it was assembled from separate pieces that were never coordinated.


So we made one commitment on Park Living:


Every decision would run through one system blueprint.


Not instinct. Not separate layers working in isolation.

One flow - every layer speaking to the others.


---

One decision changed everything.


Every conventional instinct said: lower cost, less risk, familiar ground.


But the blueprint asked a different question - not what is cheapest to build,

but what does this project need to be to deliver its full value.


We chose to follow the blueprint.


---

Same land. One connected blueprint decision.


→ Open space: 13% → 33%

→ Garden-facing units: 34% → 54%

→ Capital cycle: shortened, not stretched


The land didn't change.

The budget didn't change dramatically.


What changed was that every layer of the project

was finally working from the same intelligence.


---

That was the proof.


That when every layer of development operates through one connected system - the outcome is fundamentally different.


And then came the question:


If this is what one connected blueprint does for one project - what happens when every developer in India builds through the same foundation?


---


That question is what ROS is built to answer.

Not for one project. Not for one developer.

For every builder who already has the pieces - but has never had the architecture to connect them.
author: Chitrak Shah

title: GRI Institute India Roundtable 2026
descriptions:
During discussions at the GRI Institute India Roundtable 2026, it became clear that Ahmedabad is steadily entering the global real estate landscape.


This transition is being driven by infrastructure expansion, migration-led demand, and growing participation from institutional capital. Developments such as the Metro, Ring Road, Bullet Train corridor, and Dholera are unlocking new residential and commercial growth corridors.


Emerging micro-markets including Vaishnodevi–Zundal, Shela–Ognaj, and Bhat–Koba are demonstrating strong appreciation potential, while established markets continue to provide stability and liquidity.


Simultaneously, buyer preferences are evolving with NRIs strengthening demand for premium housing and domestic buyers placing greater emphasis on transparency, quality, and lifestyle.


The market is increasingly aligning toward integrated communities, Grade A commercial developments, and mixed-use ecosystems, supported by structured investment models and enhanced regulatory discipline through GUJRERA.


Ahmedabad’s next phase of growth will be defined by quality, governance, and long-term value creation.
author: Chitrak Shah

title: Most developers don't fail on one big problem.
descriptions:
Most developers don't fail on one big problem.

They bleed out on nine small ones - simultaneously.


---


At Shivalik, we didn't set out to build nine layers.


We built each one because a specific friction kept costing us

on every project, in every city.


And,


Park Living worked because every layer of the project spoke to each other and not in isolation.


But what are those layers?

And what does each one actually remove from a developer's problem list?


---


The Nine Layers - And What Each One Removes:


→ Blueprint - removes guesswork.

Every asset decision runs through a repeatable framework, not instinct under deadline pressure.


→ Capital - removes the funding scramble.

Structured capital engine with ₹75 Cr AIF Fund I deployed and ₹1,000+ Cr Fund II in pipeline.


→ Community - removes isolation.

15,000+ clients, 4,500+ channel partners, 500+ vendors — network that compounds with every project.


→ ROS - removes memory dependency.

Operating intelligence moves from people's heads into living architecture.


→ Pulses - removes blind spots.

Intelligence engine that feeds real data back into every planning and execution decision.


→ Institute - removes capability gaps.

1,300+ learners trained so the next generation builds with system thinking, not just transactions.


→ Development - removes reinvention.

Standardised execution protocols across every site, every city, every partner.


→ Governance - removes the handover gap.

Livability integrated at delivery so the resident experience matches the design intent.


→ Asset Management - removes value decay.

What gets built gets protected - governance continues long after handover.


---


Nine frictions. Nine layers were built to remove them.


Not as separate tools.

As one connected flow where each layer strengthens every other.


---


Most developers are already managing all nine of these areas.


The difference is not what you manage.


It is whether they run as nine separate problems -

or as One Operating System that solves them together.
author: Chitrak Shah

title: Wipro Enters GIFT City
descriptions:
Wipro has inaugurated its new office at GIFT City, Gandhinagar.


This signals a strong shift in how global companies are positioning themselves within India’s financial ecosystem.

Key developments linked to this move:


• 20+ international-standard restaurants expected in GIFT City within 1 year

• Government actively building a “Working and Living” model to retain talent

• Strong academic pipeline from IIM Ahmedabad, MICA, Nirma University and GNLU

• Foreign universities also setting up presence to support global workforce demand

• Structured internship and placement systems being aligned with GIFT ecosystem


What this means:

  • GIFT City is moving beyond infrastructure into a fully integrated ecosystem
  • Live, work, talent, capital and global business are being built in one zone
  • Policy push + corporate entry + talent pipeline = acceleration phase
  • Capital that moved abroad for decades is now reversing direction
  • High-value employment is expected to scale significantly


This is no longer a planned project

This is active execution toward a global financial hub


For real estate:

Commercial demand strengthens first

Residential absorption follows talent migration

Rental markets tighten around employment hubs

Early ecosystem entries define long-term positioning

GIFT City is entering its next growth cycle
author: Chitrak Shah

title: GIFT City – Social Infrastructure Signal
descriptions:
GIFT City is not just growing as a business hub anymore, it’s now entering the lifestyle infrastructure phase.

A new world-class school is being planned within GIFT City, spread across ~3.2–3.3 lakh sq ft, expected to be operational in the next 3 years.


What this indicates:

• Shift from work destination → liveable ecosystem

• Rising demand from working professionals, families, and global workforce

• Strong push towards long-term residential stability


Why this matters for real estate:

• Education infrastructure is a key trigger for residential demand

• Increases end-user confidence, not just investor interest

• Supports price stability and long-term appreciation

• Strengthens GIFT City’s positioning as a self-sustained urban zone



Early infrastructure signals like schools, healthcare, and community spaces define the next phase of growth.

Smart investors track these shifts early,

because once the ecosystem is complete,

the opportunity is no longer early.
author: Chitrak Shah

title: From Fast Decisions to Smart Decisions
descriptions:
Home buying today is not slower.

It’s smarter.


Earlier, buyers would finalize within 30–45 days.

Today, many take 60–90 days, often evaluating multiple projects before deciding.


What changed?

Access to information.

More options.

Higher financial awareness.

Buyers are not rushing.


They are comparing, questioning, and thinking long-term.


Which means:

Fewer impulsive decisions.

More informed decisions.

And in this shift, projects that provide clarity, transparency, and real value stand out.

Because today,


the buyer doesn’t need convincing they need confidence.
author: Chitrak Shah

title: Every Prime Location Was Once “Too Far” - Is Shantigram Next?
descriptions:
Ahmedabad has always grown in layers.

Satellite → Prahladnagar → Bopal → Shela

Each location was once considered “far” before becoming a preferred address.


Over the last 5–7 years, Bopal–Shela alone has seen nearly 2–3x expansion in residential development, driven by infrastructure, land availability, and buyer movement.


A similar shift is now visible around Shantigram and its surrounding belts.

But what’s interesting is not just the location — it’s the behaviour of the community choosing it.


Shantigram today is attracting a balanced mix of:

  • Established Gujarati families
  • Upgrading urban professionals
  • Select migrant working class
  • NRI investors


All with one common intent a more structured, long-term way of living.

Today’s buyers are not just looking for a flat.

They are choosing a better way of living.


A planned environment - where roads, zoning, and movement are designed together, not adjusted later.

Open spaces and breathing room - where there is real distance between buildings, better light, and natural ventilation.

Better lifestyle infrastructure - where schools, retail, connectivity, and daily needs are within reach, reducing everyday friction.

And an integrated community - where residential, social, and lifestyle elements work together, not in isolation.

That’s exactly why more families are moving towards ecosystems like Shantigram.


With its scale, planning, and ecosystem already in place, it is not just a development - it is shaping a complete residential micro-market.


And this is how every major hub in Ahmedabad has evolved.

Locations don’t become prime overnight.


They grow step by step and those who enter early benefit the most.

Because in real estate,

value is created during the evolution phase, not after it is already established.
author: Chitrak Shah

title: Redevelopment in Ahmedabad vs Mumbai
descriptions:
Redevelopment in Ahmedabad vs Mumbai


In recent someone asked me about redevelopment gap in Ahmedabad vs Mumbai.


And there are many things but on primary level,

In Mumbai, redevelopment became a necessity.

Land scarcity forced alignment.

Self-redevelopment evolved into a structured culture.


In Ahmedabad, urgency is lower.

We still have expansion corridors.

That’s why redevelopment here has been gradual.


There are broadly two expectations in the market:


One group focuses on better living,

better design, planning, and quality.


Another group focuses on higher benefit,

more area, stronger financial upside.


Both perspectives are valid.


The real challenge is alignment,

when multiple families must agree on timelines, compensation, structure, and long-term value.


The redevelopment journey will start accelerating in Ahmedabad.

It will grow steadily with stronger awareness, clearer processes, and institutional trust.


In this sector, credibility matters more than promises.
author: Chitrak Shah

title: How do the upper columns actually take shape on site?
descriptions:
few days ago i visited GIFT City for a site review of Curv of India.


The focus was straightforward.

When two elevated structural forms intersect,

how do the upper columns actually take shape on site?


What grade of steel is being used?

How does the plate system behave during installation?

Does the detailing feel as strong on ground as it looks on paper?


In one critical junction, we adopted a full-plate structural solution,

A relatively unique approach at this scale.


On drawings, everything is precise.

Lines are clean.

Loads are calculated.

The system feels controlled.


On site, the building has weight.

Scale.

Resistance.


You feel the structure differently when you stand beneath it.

You notice alignment challenges, handling limitations, execution realities,

Things no drawing can fully capture.


Design carries intent.

Execution carries experience.


That difference is why on-ground reviews matter.


Each site visit strengthens the feedback loop between what we imagine and what actually stands.

Between engineering logic and lived structure.


Because buildings are not just designed to look right.

They must feel right when they rise.


And without disciplined execution, no idea becomes real.
author: Chitrak Shah

title: Exactly one year ago today 26 Feb 2025, I stepped away from execution.
descriptions:

For two decades, we delivered 20 Million+ Sq Feet,

The next era of real estate will not be built by taller buildings.

title: I spent 15 years solving the wrong problems.
descriptions:
I spent 15 years solving the wrong problems.

Not bad problems. Just the wrong level of problems.


And I didn't even know there were levels.


Level 0: Not looking at it

You see it. You feel it. You look away.


"It's not that serious."

It always is.


Level 1: Solving for now

Fire burning. You grab water. Fire goes out.

Except you're not moving on. You're moving in circles.

Same problems, different month.


I built 75+ landmarks like this. Proud of every one.

But I was exhausted in a way I couldn't explain.

I was solving instances not the source.


Level 2: Solving permanently

I stopped asking -"how do I fix this project?"

And started asking, "why does this keep happening?"

Built systems. Processes that ran without me.

The work got lighter. The company got stronger.


This is where you stop being the solution and start building solutions.


Level 3: Solving for others

Everything I built inside Shivalik, other developers needed it too.

Not as competition. As infrastructure.


The industry was fragmented because everyone was solving Level 1 problems,

Alone, repeatedly without anyone building the shared foundation underneath.


The bridge: First Principles

Getting to Level 4 requires a different question entirely.

Not "how do I solve this?" but, "why does this problem exist at all?"

When I applied that to Indian real estate, the answer was uncomfortable.


The industry doesn't have a people problem.

It has an infrastructure problem.


No standards. No shared systems.

No common language between developers, buyers, capital, and cities.

That's a civilizational gap.


Level 4: Solving for the industry

Walking away from pure development, my identity for 20 years felt either visionary or delusional.

Some days it still does.

But I kept coming back to one question:


If not now, when? If not someone who's been inside this industry for 20 years - who?


That's why I'm building ROS - Real Estate Operating System.

Not a product. Not a startup.

A standard. A system. A new foundation for how real estate in India gets built.


When you solve at Level 4 - you don't just move yourself forward.

You move the city. You move the industry. You move the generation.


So where are you solving?

→ Level 0 - avoiding it

→ Level 1 - fixing it temporarily

→ Level 2 - solving it permanently

→ Level 3 - sharing the solution

→ Level 4 - eliminating the problem for everyone


The levels don't measure your worth.


They just show you where the next door is.


Spent 20 years building projects. Realised the industry needed something deeper. Now building ROS - the operating system for Indian real estate.


Building the world's largest real estate system.

Nine layers • One standard • Infinite scale.


#RealEstate #SystemsThinking #Leadership #FirstPrinciples #ROS
author: Chitrak Shah

title: Ahmedabad VS Mumbai Real Estate Developers
descriptions:
I’ve spent 20 years in real estate.

Across two cities.

And I still find myself explaining this to developers.

Mumbai and Ahmedabad are not the same market.

They never were.

· · ·

One number tells the whole story.

Price per sq ft today —

Mumbai → ₹45,000 – ₹55,000

Ahmedabad → ₹5,000 - ₹6,000

8 to 10 times difference.

But that’s not the real gap.

The real gap is in how each city thinks.

· · ·

Mumbai ran out of land decades ago.

So the entire game became - how do you extract maximum value from minimum land?

Vertical towers. FSI pushed to the limit. Redevelopment of the same plot. Again and again.

Scarcity became the product.

· · ·

Ahmedabad still has room to breathe.

So the game here is different - assemble large land parcels. Build townships. Create ecosystems around them. Play a longer cycle.

Scale became the product.

· · ·

Same 1,000 sq ft flat.

Mumbai → ₹1.3 Cr to ₹3 Cr

Ahmedabad → ₹45L to ₹70L

Same carpet area.

Completely different logic behind the price.

· · ·

Here’s what I’ve seen go wrong.

A Mumbai developer enters Ahmedabad and tries to build vertical premium towers priced at Mumbai logic.

Doesn’t work.

An Ahmedabad developer enters Mumbai thinking township scale will win.

Doesn’t work either.

The product isn’t wrong.

The playbook is.

· · ·

India’s real estate future isn’t one model.

It’s 30 cities each running their own version of this industry simultaneously.

The developers who win will be the ones who understand which game they’re actually playing.

· · ·

Mumbai monetizes scarcity.

Ahmedabad monetizes scale.

Most developers never figure out which game they’re playing.

The ones who do - build differently.
